title: Newton-Raphson Method for Numerical Equations
content:
# Newton-Raphson Method for Numerical Equations

Section: Engineering Mathematics
Topic: Numerical Methods
Importance: High (1-2 Marks in GATE AG)

## Key Concepts & Summary
The Newton-Raphson method is a powerful iterative technique for finding root approximations of real-valued functions $f(x) = 0$.

## Iteration Formula
$$x_{n+1} = x_n - \frac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}$$

## Order of Convergence & Criteria
- **Order of Convergence**: Quadratic (Order $2$). The error at step $n+1$ is proportional to the square of the error at step $n$:
  $$\epsilon_{n+1} \approx C \cdot \epsilon_n^2$$
- **Condition for Convergence**: Method converges provided $f'(x) \ne 0$ near the root and $|f(x) \cdot f''(x)| < |f'(x)|^2$.

## Key Exam Pitfalls
1. If $f'(x_n) = 0$, the tangent is horizontal and Newton-Raphson fails (division by zero).
2. For multiple roots, convergence drops from quadratic (Order 2) to linear (Order 1).

title: IC Engine Efficiencies and Power Parameters
topic: Farm Power and Machinery Core Concepts
content:
# IC Engine Efficiencies and Power Parameters

Section: Farm Power and Machinery
Topic: Sources of Farm Power — IC Engines
Importance: High (2-3 Marks in GATE AG)

## Key Concepts & Summary
Internal Combustion (IC) Engines convert chemical energy of fuel into mechanical work. Understanding the relationship between Indicated Power (IP), Brake Power (BP), Friction Power (FP), and Mechanical Efficiency ($\eta_{mech}$) is essential for solving GATE numericals.

## Essential Formulas
- **Indicated Power (IP)**:
  $$IP = \frac{P_{m} \cdot L \cdot A \cdot N \cdot n}{60000} \quad \text{[kW]}$$
  Where $P_m$ is mean effective pressure (kPa or $\text{N/m}^2$), $L$ is stroke length (m), $A$ is piston area ($\text{m}^2$), $N$ is RPM (working strokes per min), and $n$ is number of cylinders.
  *Note for 4-stroke engine: $N = \text{RPM} / 2$; for 2-stroke engine: $N = \text{RPM}$.*

- **Brake Power (BP)**:
  $$BP = \frac{2\pi \cdot N \cdot T}{60000} = \frac{2\pi \cdot N \cdot (W - S) \cdot R}{60000} \quad \text{[kW]}$$

- **Friction Power (FP)**:
  $$FP = IP - BP$$

- **Mechanical Efficiency ($\eta_{mech}$)**:
  $$\eta_{mech} = \frac{BP}{IP} \times 100\%$$

- **Brake Thermal Efficiency ($\eta_{bt}$)**:
  $$\eta_{bt} = \frac{BP}{m_f \cdot CV} \times 100\%$$
  Where $m_f$ is fuel consumption rate ($\text{kg/s}$) and $CV$ is calorific value ($\text{kJ/kg}$).

- **Specific Fuel Consumption (SFC)**:
  $$SFC = \frac{m_f}{BP} \quad \text{[kg / kW}\cdot\text{h]}$$

## Key Takeaways & Exam Tips
1. Always convert fuel consumption to $\text{kg/s}$ and $CV$ to $\text{kJ/kg}$ before applying the thermal efficiency formula.
2. For 4-stroke engines, power stroke occurs once every 2 crankshaft revolutions ($N = \text{rpm}/2$).
3. Weight transfer on tractor chassis increases tractive efficiency on rear drive wheels.

title: Universal Soil Loss Equation (USLE)
topic: Soil and Water Conservation Engineering Core Concepts
content:
# Universal Soil Loss Equation (USLE)

Section: Soil and Water Conservation Engineering
Topic: Soil Erosion & Conservation Engineering
Importance: High (2 Marks in GATE AG)

## Key Concepts & Summary
The Universal Soil Loss Equation (USLE) is an empirical model developed by Wischmeier and Smith (1978) to estimate long-term average annual soil loss caused by sheet and rill erosion.

## Essential Formula
$$A = R \cdot K \cdot L \cdot S \cdot C \cdot P$$

Where:
- **$A$**: Computed average annual soil loss per unit area ($\text{tonnes / ha / year}$).
- **$R$**: Rainfall and runoff erosivity factor ($\text{MJ}\cdot\text{mm / ha}\cdot\text{h}\cdot\text{year}$).
- **$K$**: Soil erodibility factor ($\text{tonnes}\cdot\text{ha}\cdot\text{h / ha}\cdot\text{MJ}\cdot\text{mm}$).
- **$L$**: Topographic slope-length factor (dimensionless ratio).
- **$S$**: Topographic slope-steepness factor (dimensionless ratio).
- **$C$**: Cover and crop management factor ($0 \le C \le 1$).
- **$P$**: Conservation support practice factor ($0 \le P \le 1$, $P = 1$ for up-and-down slope tillage without conservation practice).

## Topographic Factor ($LS$)
Combined slope length ($L$) and steepness ($S$) factor formula:
$$LS = \left( \frac{\lambda}{22.13} \right)^m \left( 65.41 \sin^2\theta + 4.56 \sin\theta + 0.065 \right)$$
Where $\lambda$ is slope length (m), $\theta$ is slope angle, and $m$ is exponent ($0.5$ for slopes $\ge 5\%$).

## Exam Tips
1. Note that $L$, $S$, $C$, and $P$ are dimensionless factors! Only $A$, $R$, and $K$ carry dimensional units.
2. If conservation practices like contour bunding or strip cropping are used, $P < 1.0$. If no practice is used, $P = 1.0$.

title: Farmstead Location And Design Medium
content:
Importance of Location Selection for a Farmstead and Facilities in Farm House Design

(UPSC — IFoS Perspective)

Introduction

A farmstead is the operational nucleus of the farm business, comprising the farm house together with allied structures such as livestock sheds, storage, and machinery houses. Since the site and layout are rarely changed once established, careful location selection and functional design are essential to minimise cost, labour, and drudgery over the entire productive life of the farm.

Factors Influencing Farmstead Location — At a Glance

Importance of Location Selection

Topography: Elevated, gently sloping land (1–3%) ensures natural drainage and avoids water-logging or flooding during monsoons.

Soil conditions: Firm, well-drained soil with good bearing capacity prevents foundation cracks and seepage into wells and storage pits.

Water supply: An assured, potable source is essential for domestic use, livestock, and farm operations; water table should be checked for well/bore-well feasibility.

Accessibility: Proximity to an all-weather road eases transport of inputs, produce, and access to markets, schools, and health facilities.

Centrality: A central location within the land holding reduces travel time and labour cost for workers, animals, and machinery.

Drainage and flood safety: The site must be free from flood risk, with provision for natural or artificial drainage of rain and farm waste.

Orientation and climate: Proper aspect ensures winter sunlight, summer shade, and ventilation; windbreaks protect against prevailing winds and soil erosion.

Power supply: Nearness to the electricity grid supports irrigation pumps, lighting, and small-scale processing at lower cost.

Sanitation: The site should avoid swampy or insect-infested areas and allow safe disposal of waste without contaminating water sources.

Cost, legal status and expansion: Affordable land with clear title and sufficient surrounding space allows for future growth of the farm business.

Dimensioned Farmstead Layout Plan

A model layout on a 145 m × 105 m plot, drawn to indicate realistic building sizes and minimum sanitary separation distances (house–cattle shed ≥ 30 m; house–poultry ≥ 20 m; poultry–cattle shed > 15 m; well–manure pit >> 15 m), with the residence sited upwind of the livestock and waste zones.

Key Facilities in Farm House Design

Residence: Simple, durable living space built with locally available materials, with a veranda for supervising farm activities.

Livestock housing: Well-ventilated, separate sheds for dairy animals and poultry, close enough for convenience but positioned to avoid odour and fly nuisance.

Storage facilities: Rat-proof and moisture-proof grain godowns, a secure machinery/implement shed, and a separate lockable store for fertilizers and agro-chemicals.

Water supply and sanitation: Piped water from a protected well or overhead tank, with proper drainage and a soak-pit/septic system for waste disposal.

Energy facilities: Electrification for lighting and pumping, supplemented where feasible by biogas (from cattle dung) or solar units.

Internal roads: An all-weather approach lane connecting the farm house to the public road and to different field blocks.

Kitchen garden and orchard: A small plot near the house for growing vegetables and fruit for home consumption and nutrition.

Processing/value-addition space: A threshing floor and drying yard, and where feasible a small shed for grading and packing produce.

Security: Boundary fencing or hedging with adequate outdoor lighting to guard against theft and stray animals.

Expansion space: Layout should reserve land for additional structures as the farm business diversifies over time.

Conclusion

A scientifically sited and well-designed farmstead — with assured water and power, good accessibility, and functionally zoned residential, livestock, and storage facilities — ensures efficient use of labour, capital, and time, making it a key theme in farm management and rural development.
formulas: Topography: Elevated, gently sloping land (1–3%) ensures natural drainage and avoids water-logging or flooding during monsoons.
Soil conditions: Firm, well-drained soil with good bearing capacity prevents foundation cracks and seepage into wells and storage pits.
Water supply: An assured, potable source is essential for domestic use, livestock, and farm operations; water table should be checked for well/bore-well feasibility.
Accessibility: Proximity to an all-weather road eases transport of inputs, produce, and access to markets, schools, and health facilities.
Centrality: A central location within the land holding reduces travel time and labour cost for workers, animals, and machinery.
Drainage and flood safety: The site must be free from flood risk, with provision for natural or artificial drainage of rain and farm waste.

title: SIZE REDUCTION & MILLING
content:
SIZE REDUCTION & MILLING

Detailed GATE Agricultural Engineering (AG) Notes

Section 6/7 — Agricultural Process Engineering

Compiled from lecture slides: cleaning/size-reduction principles, size-reduction laws, machinery, and rice milling

Contents at a Glance

Milling — meaning and scope

Size reduction — definition, objectives, advantages

Fineness modulus and average particle size

Factors affecting size reduction

Mechanisms of size reduction

Principles & crushing efficiency

Size reduction laws — Rittinger's, Kick's, Bond's (with solved numericals)

Size reduction machinery — crushers, grinders, cutting machines

Oil expression and extraction

Rice milling — parboiling, milling equipment, flow

Quick-revision formula sheet

1. Milling — Overview

Milling is a general trade term for the reduction of food grains into end products usable for consumption or further processing.

Milling includes:

Cleaning

Sorting

Polishing

Dehusking

Size reduction

The exact meaning of "milling" varies from crop to crop — e.g. rice milling emphasises dehusking and polishing, while wheat milling emphasises grinding into flour.

2. Size Reduction — Definition & Objectives

Definition

Size reduction is the operation of reducing bigger particles into smaller ones of desired size and shape using external forces.

Size = physical dimensions of an object

Reduction = process of decreasing that size

COMMINUTION is the alternate technical term for size reduction

Objectives of Size Reduction

Increase surface area — reaction rate for solid-particle reactions is directly proportional to contact area with the second phase

Break material into small particles to separate valuable constituents

Achieve intimate mixing of two or more solids

Dispose of solid wastes easily

Improve handling characteristics of the material

Advantages of Size Reduction

Content uniformity

Uniform flow

Effective drying

Increased surface area / increased viscosity

Uniform mixing and drying

Improved rate of absorption (smaller particles → greater absorption)

Improved dissolution rate

3. Fineness Modulus (FM)

Fineness modulus indicates the uniformity of grind in the resultant product.

Determination

FM is obtained by adding the weight fractions retained above each sieve in a stack and dividing the cumulative sum by 100.

Average Particle Size

Dp = 0.135 × (1.366)^FM     (Dp in mm)

GATE tip: Dp increases roughly exponentially with FM — memorize the constants 0.135 and 1.366 exactly; GATE numericals often ask you to back-calculate FM from a given Dp or vice-versa.

Fig. Relationship between fineness modulus and average particle size

Solved Problem — Determination of Fineness Modulus

A sieve analysis gave the following weight retained on each IS sieve. Determine the fineness modulus and average particle size.

Fineness modulus, FM = 274.03 / 100 = 2.7403

Dp = 0.135 × (1.366)^2.7403 ≈ 0.317 mm

4. Factors Affecting Size Reduction

GATE tip: The 5–50% moisture "caking zone" is a favourite objective-type question — remember grinding is efficient OUTSIDE this band, not inside it.

5. Mechanisms of Size Reduction

Fig. Impact, attrition, shear, and compression mechanisms

6. Principles of Size Reduction

Crushers and grinders are the equipment mostly used for size reduction. An ideal size reducer should have:

Large capacity

Ability to yield a pre-desired product or range of sizes

Small power requirement per unit product handled

Easy and trouble-free operation

Crushing Efficiency

Crushing efficiency = Surface energy created by crushing / Energy absorbed by the solid

7. Size Reduction Theories (Energy Laws)

Energy requirement for particle size reduction is a function of the input and output particle size, hardness, strength, and other properties of the solid. Three classical theories relate energy to particle size — Rittinger's Law, Kick's Law, and Bond's Law.

General differential form

Fig. 5.3 — Reduction of feed to a symmetrical smaller particle

dE = − c · (dX / X^n)

where E = energy, X = particle size, c = constant, and n depends on the theory (n = 2 for Rittinger, n = 1 for Kick, n = 1.5 for Bond).

Fig. Particle size reduction stages vs dispersion energy — from large agglomerates down to particle fragments

7.1 Rittinger's Law (n = 2)

Work required in crushing is proportional to the new surface area created

Assumes size reduction is a shearing process

Energy requirement is proportional to the square of the common linear dimension

E = c ( 1/Xp − 1/Xf )

where Xp and Xf = length of product and feed, respectively.

7.2 Kick's Law (n = 1)

Based on stress analysis of plastic deformation within the elastic limit

Assumes energy requirement is a function of the common linear dimension of the material

Within the elastic limit, work required to crush a given quantity of material is constant for the same reduction ratio, irrespective of the original size

Reduction ratio = ratio of feed opening to discharge opening

E = c · ln (Xf / Xp)

7.3 Bond's Law

Estimates the power required for crushing and grinding operations

Work required to form particles of size Dp from a very large feed is proportional to the square root of the surface-to-volume ratio of the product

P/f = 0.3162 · wi · ( 1/√Dp − 1/√Df )

where P = power (kW), f = feed rate (t/h), Dp = sieve opening through which 80% of product passes (mm), Df = sieve opening through which 80% of feed passes (mm), wi = work index.

Work index (wi): the gross energy requirement in kWh per tonne of feed needed to reduce a very large feed to a size such that 80% of the product passes through a 100 μm screen. wi is found experimentally from laboratory crushing/grinding tests.

GATE tip: Bond's Law is the most commonly examined of the three because it is closest to industrial practice — make sure the 0.3162 constant and the "80% passing" definition of Dp/Df are second nature.

Solved Problem 1 — Rittinger's and Kick's Law

In a wheat milling experiment it was found that to grind 4.33 mm sized grains to IS sieve 30 (0.351 mm opening), the power required was 8 kW. Calculate the power requirement for milling wheat grains to IS sieve 13 (0.157 mm opening) using (i) Rittinger's Law and (ii) Kick's Law. Feed rate of milling = 200 kg/hr.

(i) According to Rittinger's Law:

E = c ( 1/Xp − 1/Xf )

8/0.2 = c (1/0.351 − 1/4.33)  ⇒  40 = c (2.619)  ⇒  c = 15.278

Putting the value of c for the second condition:

P/0.2 = 15.278 (1/0.157 − 1/4.33)

P = 18.75 kW

(ii) According to Kick's Law:

E = c · ln (Xf / Xp)

8/0.2 = c · ln(4.33/0.351)  ⇒  40 = c (2.5107)  ⇒  c = 15.93

Putting the value of c for the second condition:

P/0.2 = 15.93 · ln(4.33/0.157)

P = 10.56 kW

Solved Problem 2 — Bond's Law

How much power is required to crush 2 t/hr of a material if 80% of the feed passes through IS sieve No. 480 (4.75 mm opening) and 80% of the product passes through IS sieve No. 50 (0.5 mm opening)? Work index of the material = 6.30.

P/f = 0.3162 · wi ( 1/√Dp − 1/√Df )

Given: wi = 6.30, f = 2 t/hr, Dp = 0.50 mm, Df = 4.75 mm

P/2 = 0.3162 × 6.30 ( 1/√0.5 − 1/√4.75 )

P = 7.129 kW

8. Size Reduction Machinery

Size reduction machinery is broadly grouped into three classes: Crushers, Grinders, and Cutting machines.

8.1 Crushers

Squeeze the material until it breaks; break large pieces into small lumps

Mainly used in mining-type industries

Types: jaw crusher, gyratory crusher, crushing rolls (smooth and serrated)

Working mechanisms: compression, impact, and shearing

8.2 Grinders

Used to mill grains into powder

Types: attrition mill, hammer mill, ball mill

Ball Mill — Centrifuging & Critical Speed

Centrifuging occurs beyond a critical rotational speed of the mill.

nc = (1 / 2π) × √( g / (R − r) )

where nc = critical speed (revolutions/s), g = acceleration due to gravity (9.80 m/s²), R = radius of the mill (m), r = radius of the ball (m).

GATE tip: Operating speed for ball mills is normally kept at 65–80% of critical speed — lower values are used for wet grinding in viscous suspension. This range (65–80%) is a frequently tested fact.

8.3 Cutting Machines

Usually used for making slices of fruits and vegetables

Types: rotary knife cutter, Reitz mill (disintegrator)

9. Oil Expression and Extraction

Used to extract oil from oilseeds such as sunflower, mustard, groundnut, etc.

Mechanical Expression

Hydraulic press, screw press

Chemical-free process

Solvent (Chemical) Extraction

Uses a low-boiling-point solvent to extract oil through diffusion

High extraction efficiency (~99%), more protein retained, better preservation quality

Solvent is recovered from the cake by heating (evaporation)

Low toxicity of the solvents used

10. Rice Milling

Overall flow

Paddy → Cleaner → Storage → Sheller / Husk aspirator → Paddy separator → Whitener/Polisher → Grader → Bran aspirator → Head rice, Brokens, Bran, Bagging/Storage.

Fig. Basic flow chart of rice processing in a modern mill

Parboiling

An optional treatment given to paddy before milling. Paddy grain is composed of starch granules whose voids are filled with air/moisture.

Objective: maximize recovery of head rice and minimize breakage.

Soaking — in normal or hot water for some time

Steaming — temperature raised up to ~70°C

Drying — slow drying, usually in shade or in mechanical dryers

Advantages of Parboiling

Increases milling yield, improves quality, makes grain structure vitreous and shiny, increases shelf life

Grains harden — greater resistance to insect attack, no germination, no atmospheric adsorption

More oil in bran, easier shelling, more digestible

Less sticky, swells more

Absorbs less oil during cooking; doesn't turn rancid easily after cooking

Disadvantages of Parboiling

Heat treatment destroys natural antioxidants; rancidity may develop during long-term storage

Rice takes more time to cook and develops a peculiar off-flavour

Extra capital investment (drying equipment)

More power required during polishing

Longer soaking time makes paddy prone to attack by spores

Parboiling Methods

Head Rice vs Broken Rice

Head rice: kernel length > 3/4 of the whole grain

Broken rice: kernel length < 3/4 of the whole grain

Broken rice is further classified as:

Big brokens — 50–75% of kernel length

Small brokens — 12.5–50% of kernel length

Points — < 12.5% of kernel length

Traditional milling equipment includes hand and foot pounders.

Rice Milling / Dehusking Equipment

Fig. 5.25 — Engleberg huller (1. hulling roller 2. screen 3. knife 4. balancing pulley 5. casing 6. straight ribs 7. spiral ribs)

Fig. 5.28 — Rubber-roll sheller

Fig. 5.26 — Under-runner disk huller

Other Milling Operations

Husk separator

Paddy separator (compartment type)

Whitening — horizontal and vertical whitening cones, jet pearlers

Glazing

Grading — using indent-cylinder separators

GATE tip: Yield hierarchy to remember: rubber-roll sheller (~95%) > Engleberg huller (56–64%). GATE frequently tests this ranking along with the huller's rpm range (600–900 rpm).

11. Quick-Revision Formula Sheet

Key numbers to remember

Moisture caking range where grinding is poor: 5–50%

Ball mill operating speed: 65–80% of critical speed (lower for wet/viscous grinding)

Engleberg huller speed: 600–900 rpm; yield 56–64%

Rubber roll sheller yield: up to 95%; roll speed differential ≈ 25%

CFTRI parboiling: soak 3–4 h at 85°C water heated by steam

Pressure parboiling: soak 40 min at 85°C + pressurized steam for 18 min

Bond's work index (wi) definition: energy (kWh/tonne) to reduce very large feed so 80% of product passes a 100 μm screen

End of notes — Size Reduction & Milling (GATE AG).

Size = physical dimensions of an object
Reduction = process of decreasing that size
GATE tip: Dp increases roughly exponentially with FM — memorize the constants 0.135 and 1.366 exactly; GATE numericals often ask you to back-calculate FM from a given Dp or vice-versa.

title: Psychrometrics & Grain Drying Principles
content:
# Psychrometrics & Grain Drying Principles

Section: Agricultural Process Engineering
Topic: Processing Operations — Psychrometrics & Drying
Importance: High (2 Marks in GATE AG)

## Key Concepts & Summary
Psychrometrics is the study of moist air thermodynamic properties. Grain drying involves simultaneous heat and mass transfer where moisture migrates from the interior of grain to the surface and evaporates into air.

## Important Definitions & Moisture Bases
- **Dry Basis Moisture Content ($M_{db}$)**:
  $$M_{db} = \frac{m_w}{m_d} \times 100\%$$
  Where $m_w$ is mass of water and $m_d$ is mass of dry matter.

- **Wet Basis Moisture Content ($M_{wb}$)**:
  $$M_{wb} = \frac{m_w}{m_w + m_d} \times 100\%$$

- **Inter-conversion Formulas**:
  $$M_{db} = \frac{M_{wb}}{100 - M_{wb}} \times 100$$
  $$M_{wb} = \frac{M_{db}}{100 + M_{db}} \times 100$$

## Thin Layer Drying Equation (Lewis Model)
$$\frac{M - M_e}{M_0 - M_e} = \exp(-k \cdot t)$$
Where:
- $M$: Moisture content at time $t$
- $M_0$: Initial moisture content
- $M_e$: Equilibrium moisture content (EMC)
- $k$: Drying constant ($\text{hr}^{-1}$)
- $t$: Drying time ($\text{hr}$)

## Exam Tips
1. Dry matter mass ($m_d$) remains constant during drying operations! Use $m_{d1} = m_{d2}$ to solve grain weight loss problems quickly:
   $$W_1 (1 - M_{wb1}) = W_2 (1 - M_{wb2})$$
2. Always check whether given moisture content is on Wet Basis or Dry Basis before applying formulas.

title: Probability Distributions & Aptitude Ratios
content:
# Probability Distributions & Aptitude Ratios

Section: General Aptitude
Topic: Quantitative Aptitude
Importance: High (2 Marks in GATE AG)

## Key Concepts & Summary
General Aptitude questions in GATE test logical clarity, ratio applications, and standard probability models (Binomial, Poisson, Normal).

## Essential Formulas
- **Binomial Distribution**:
  $$P(X = k) = \binom{n}{k} p^k (1-p)^{n-k}$$
  Mean $\mu = n p$, Variance $\sigma^2 = n p (1-p)$.

- **Poisson Distribution**:
  $$P(X = k) = \frac{\lambda^k e^{-\lambda}}{k!}$$
  Mean $\mu = \lambda$, Variance $\sigma^2 = \lambda$.

- **Work and Time Ratio**:
  $$\text{Work} = \text{Rate} \times \text{Time}$$
  If $A$ takes $T_A$ days and $B$ takes $T_B$ days, together they take:
  $$T_{combined} = \frac{T_A \cdot T_B}{T_A + T_B}$$
formulas: Mean $\mu = n p$, Variance $\sigma^2 = n p (1-p)$.
